title: SPORTSBOOK BEHAVIOR IN THE NCAA FOOTBALL BETTING MARKET: TESTS OF THE TRADITIONAL AND LEVITT MODELS OF SPORTSBOOK BEHAVIOR
items.abstract: <jats:p>The predictions of the traditional balanced-book sportsbook model and the alternative Levitt model of sportsbook behavior are tested using actual betting percentages on the favorite/underdog and over/under for NCAA Football.  Sportsbooks are found to not balance betting dollars, which is in contradiction to the assumptions of the traditional models of sportsbook behavior.  In the pointspread market, more bets are placed on the favorite in contests with road favorites and in games with higher pointspreads.  In the totals market, more bets are placed on the over as the total increases and in games on television.  Some support is found for the Levitt model of sportsbook behavior, as sportsbooks appear to price to maximize profits when the behavioral biases of bettors are clear, such as games with road favorites and games with the highest pointspreads and totals.  In all other contests, however, the sportsbook appears to price as a forecast, as each proposition wins half of the time, even in the presence of betting imbalances.</jats:p>

title: Should the Rules Be Different When Prediction Markets Play Sportsbook?
items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid expansion of U.S. prediction market platforms has triggered a complex legal debate over whether event contracts functioning as sports wagers should be regulated under federal derivatives law or state gambling frameworks. While information-driven markets aggregate valuable macroeconomic data and facilitate financial hedging, sports contracts on platforms like Kalshi largely serve as mass-market recreational wagering. The author advocates for a functional regulatory approach that distinguishes contracts based on their actual economic purpose rather than their shared technological mechanics.</jats:p>

title: Mistiming is not Arbitrage: A Pre-registered Falsification of Cross-platform Prediction-market Arbitrage, and the Two-sided Cancellation of the Favourite-longshot Premium
items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent work reports a persistent, structurally protected arbitrage between the two largest prediction-market venues. We test it on executable quotes, Kalshi one-minute bid/ask candlesticks joined to the full Polymarket CLOB archive across 855 deterministically matched MLB moneylines and all four strikes of the June 2026 Federal Reserve decision, and find none. At true alignment the median cross-venue mid divergence is 0.60¢ against a 2.00¢ Kalshi fee, and only 7.03% of 20,915 aligned minutes carry a fee-clearing edge, with a median life of one minute. A mistiming sweep identifies the artifact: deliberately shifting one venue's quotes against the other makes the apparent edge grow monotonically, 7.03% → 23.8% at seven minutes on the fast panel, and 22.7% → 40.8% at sixty minutes on the slow one, where the mean net edge turns positive only at an hour of mistiming. The cleanest windows, pre-game minutes, are profitable in 0.00% of 2,617 minutes. We further show that the favourite-longshot premium is cancelled on both sides of the book: takers pay a half-spread five to seven times the fee, while makers who avoid it realise −7.39¢ per contract (t = −13.6), because fills arrive only when they are losing. Across nine pre-registered theses no fee- and spread-clearing edge survives. All results are pre-registered and reproducible from committed one-command scripts.</jats:p>

title: Same Bet, Different Markets: Cross-Market Pricing Anomalies and the Limits of Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
items.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the pricing relationship between two prediction markets trading on an identical binary event: the passage of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act by December 31, 2026. One market, Kalshi, operates as a Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)regulated exchange serving U.S. customers. The other, Polymarket, is an unregulated global platform settled in cryptocurrency. Despite trading on the same event with the same resolution criteria, the two markets exhibit a correlation of only 0.55 for probability levels and 0.22 for daily changes, with spreads reaching 26.1 percentage points. A mean-reversion trading strategy that enters when the spread exceeds 10 percentage points and exits at zero generates a 100% win rate across 9 trades between January and May 2026, with an average net return of 15.6% per trade and a mean holding period of 5.9 days. A secondary analysis tests whether these prediction market probabilities explain Bitcoin daily returns and finds no significant relationship for either market. The findings provide evidence that regulatory market segmentation creates persistent, tradable pricing anomalies in prediction markets, and that these anomalies are likely to diminish as Polymarket gains CFTC-licensed access to U.S. customers.</jats:p>

title: The Relationship between Sportsbook Volume, Forecast Accuracy, and Market Efficiency:  The NFL and NCAA Football
items.abstract: <jats:p>Using betting market volume data for the NFL and NCAA Football, we examine the role of betting volume as it relates to bettor biases, forecast accuracy, and volume-based betting market strategies.  We find that betting volume has a statistically significant effect on the percentage bet on the favorite, but its impact is different between the two levels of football.  Increased betting volume was shown to not have an impact on forecast accuracy in the sports.  Simple betting simulations revealed that underdogs win more than implied by efficiency in low-volume NFL games, but other strategies did not reject market efficiency.</jats:p>

Arbitrage and Risk Arbitrage in the Nikkei Put Warrant Market
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper develops useful theory of arbitrage and risk arbitrage. It describes a prize winning successful risk arbitrage involving Nikkei put warrants trading on the Toronto and American stock exchanges. The paper describes the various types of contracts and how the risk arbitrage was traded and executed.</jats:p>

Decision-aware stress conformal prediction for battery arbitrage in day-ahead electricity markets: a CatBoost NBEATSx ensemble and seven-market study
items.abstract: <jats:p>​Day-ahead electricity price forecasting is increasingly evaluated not only by statistical accuracy but also by the operational value it creates for flexible assets. This paper develops a decision aware conformal framework for battery arbitrage that calibrates downside risk at the level of the scheduled action rather than at the level of hourly price intervals. The forecasting layer benchmarks CatBoost, LightGBM, NBEATSx, N-HiTS, and Temporal Fusion Transformers (TFT) on a public seven-market dataset covering Germany and six Italian price zones. The operational layer uses a 24h linear battery scheduling model with state-of-charge dynamics, round-trip efficiency, power and energy limits, and a linear degradation penalty. On top of the point forecast, the proposed ProfitGuardStressCP method estimates a rolling, stress-conditioned one-sided lower bound on point-schedule profit using range-scaled optimism errors. The method is benchmarked against two conformal operational baselines based on hour-wise residual calibration: a robust linear program and a scenario-CVaR scheduler. Within the compact, trainingfair benchmark, the CatBoost–NBEATSx ensemble attains the lowest average forecast MAE, 3.540 EUR/MWh, across the seven markets. Embedded in the realistic battery model, the point ensemble attains the highest mean realized profit of 21.070 EUR/day. ProfitGuardStressCP preserves 97.8% of that profit while reducing loss days from 73 to 29 over 1,824 market-days, and achieves empirical lower-bound coverage of 0.906 against a nominal 0.90 target. The results show that calibrating decision-level profit optimism yields a more attractive profit-risk trade-off than hour-wise conformal interval methods when the end use is battery arbitrage.</jats:p>

title: Latency Arbitrage and Market Liquidity1
items.abstract: <jats:p>There is an increasing concern that fast arbitrageurs make liquidity more expensive by picking off quotes before the market makers can revise them. This paper shows that restricting aggressive proprietary trading mitigates adverse selection and improves liquidity. Specifically, by restricting aggressive proprietary trading, adverse selection costs measured by permanent price movement decline by 21%, and liquidity measured by bid-ask spread declines by 11%. Liquidity providers earn higher realized spreads and quote higher volumes at better prices. In addition, this paper shows that the restriction eliminates more than half of cross-exchange toxic arbitrage trades. Market makers benefit from a lower likelihood of being sniped when public information arrives and therefore take on lower selection costs. These findings suggest that restricting latency arbitrage improves liquidity by reducing toxic arbitrage.</jats:p>

title: Market Efficiency, Arbitrage and the NYMEX Crude Oil Futures Market
items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Since Engle and Granger formulated the concept of cointegration in 1987, the literature has extensively examined the unbiasedness of the commodity futures prices using the cointegration-based technique. Despite intense attention, many of the previous studies suffer from the contradicting empirical results. That is, the cointegration test and the stationarity test on the differential contradict each other. In marked contrast, my dissertation develops the no-arbitrage cost-of-carry model in the NYMEX light sweet crude oil futures market and tests stationarity of the spot-futures differential. It is demonstrated that the primary cause of the "cointegration paradox" is the model misspecifications resulting in omitted variable bias.</jats:p>

title: Market Imperfections, Equilibrium and Arbitrage
items.abstract: <jats:p>The theory of asset pricing, which takes its roots in the Arrow-Debreu model, the Black and Scholes formula, has been famalized in a framework by Harrison and Kreps (1979), harrison and Pliska (1979) and Kreps (1981). In these models, securities markets are assumed to be frictionless. The main result is that a price process is arbitrage free (or, equivalently, compatible with some equilibrium) if and only if it is, when appropriately renormalized, a martingale for some equivalent probability measure. The theory of pricing by arbitrage flows from there. Contingent claims can be priced by taking their expected value with respect to an equivalent martingale measure. If this value is unique, the claim is said to be priced by arbitrage. The new probabilities can be interpreted as state prices or as the intertemporal marginal ratyes of substitution of an agent maximizing his expected utility. In this work, we will propose a general model that takes frictions into account.</jats:p>
